node.label: Janet L. (Jinty) Nelson
node.date_label: Politics and Ritual (1986) · Charles the Bald (1992) · The Frankish World (1996) · “Gendering Courts” (2004) · King and Emperor (2019; Penguin paperback 2020)
node.description: In Charles the Bald (1992), Nelson explains Carolingian government through cooperation between kings, aristocrats and churchmen, challenging accounts that treat their power as necessarily competing. Politics and Ritual in Early Medieval Europe (1986) places ritual within the exercise and communication of political authority. Her work on queens, courts and masculinity makes women and gender integral to political explanation. King and Emperor (2019) follows Charlemagne chronologically, seeking the person behind the accumulated legend through close reading of fragmentary sources. Andrew J. Romig praised its source criticism but questioned its limited examination of Frankish identity and the way its biographical frame can become a general history of the period. Julia M. H. Smith praised the argument of “Gendering Courts” while judging as over-reach its inference, from the sources’ silence about Aachen’s baths after Charlemagne, that serious conversation moved from the baths to mixed-gender spaces such as the hall and the hunt.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Politics and Ritual in Early Medieval Europe (1986), including “Queens as Jezebels” (original 1978); Charles the Bald (1992); The Frankish World, 750–900 (1996); “Monks, Secular Men and Masculinity, c. 900” (1999); “Gendering Courts in the Early Medieval West” (2004); Gender and Historiography (2012), coedited with Susan Reynolds and Susan Johns; King and Emperor: A New Life of Charlemagne (2019; Penguin paperback 2020).
node.scope_note: Selected passages in Stafford’s memoir and the 2025 collective tribute, the IHR interview, Romig’s review, the KCL bibliography and the licensed King and Emperor preview were read. Preview reading covers preliminary publication material and introduction pp. 1–8, not the complete book. Earlier monographs, collected essays and the 2012 coedited volume remain unread in full; Scott and Weber applications and the Elias/Foucault criticisms are documented through named readers.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her IHR interview (2008), Nelson names Peter Brown, whose work she says took medieval history into cultural and social history, as “the third great influence on me”, as a reader of his work rather than a student.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: IHR transcript, answer beginning “But neither of those two”, through “third great influence on me, Peter Brown” (web lines 95–101): she places herself among Brown’s readers, not his students, and discusses his questions about religious belief and saints. Brown’s books were not newly read; no supervision relationship asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Stafford documents, Nelson invokes Marc Bloch’s injunction to seek people behind historical evidence in “Monks, Secular Men and Masculinity, c. 900” (1999).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stafford, printed p. 24, paragraph beginning “And it was here”, n. 55, identifies Nelson’s invocation of Bloch and locates the essay passage at p. 138. Her phrase “real men” expresses the methodological point. Mediated evidence: the 1999 essay and Bloch’s original were not read directly.
proposed_edges.map_label: Bloch and people behind the sources

proposed_edges.relationship: According to Stafford, Nelson applies James C. Scott’s Seeing Like a State (1998) to Charlemagne’s unsuccessful canal project in King and Emperor (2019).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stafford, printed p. 28, second sentence and n. 74, explicitly names Scott and locates Nelson’s application at King and Emperor, pp. 295–296. This is a specific application documented by a named scholarly reader; those pages and Scott’s book are unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Stafford reports, Nelson uses a Weberian pointsman metaphor for Charlemagne’s capacity to redirect ideas in King and Emperor (2019).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stafford, printed p. 28, opening paragraph, n. 75, calls the figure “Weberian” and cites King and Emperor, pp. 292 and 285. Limited to this metaphor; no general Weberian affiliation. Those book pages and the originating Weber passage are unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Julia M. H. Smith’s reading, “Gendering Courts in the Early Medieval West” (2004) challenges Elias’s male-centred court model by placing women within early medieval courtliness.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Smith, in Rio et al. (2025), printed p. 321, paragraph beginning “It takes something of an effort”, names Elias, quotes Nelson’s criticism of a world consisting “of men only”, and explains her earlier chronology and women’s agency. The 2004 chapter, pp. 185–197, remains unread directly. The claim follows Smith’s specific reading, not an independently established refutation of all Elias.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Julia M. H. Smith documents, Nelson criticizes Foucault’s neglect of women in “Gendering Courts in the Early Medieval West” (2004).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Smith, Rio et al. (2025), printed p. 321, same court-studies paragraph: Foucault is explicitly one of the two writers criticized. Limited to omission of women; neither rejection of genealogy nor a debt to Foucault inferred. Nelson’s chapter and the relevant Foucault books remain unread directly.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Queens as Jezebels” (1978), as Stafford explains, makes royal women’s action part of the explanation of early medieval political power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stafford, printed pp. 20–23, especially p. 20 n. 38 (1978 original) and p. 22 on integrating women into political history. This concerns interpretation of queens and power, not a claim of equal status or unrestricted agency. Original essay unread; Politics and Ritual (1986) is the reprint collection, not the essay’s original date.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Stafford explains, “Monks, Secular Men and Masculinity, c. 900” (1999) examines tensions between aristocratic masculine duties and Christian demands.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stafford, printed pp. 23–24, nn. 52–55, describes violence, reproduction and monastic masculinity as historically situated pressures. Original essay unread; its 2007 collection does not replace the original 1999 publication. This is a specific gender-history contribution, not a generic field-membership inference.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her IHR interview (2008), Nelson, author of Politics and Ritual in Early Medieval Europe (1986), describes the early medieval study of ritual as tied to cultural history, so that ritual and the activities of legislative assemblies are seen as “both real” and “constantly interacting”.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: IHR transcript, answers to the cultural-turn questions (web lines 169–176), particularly the interaction of ritual with legislative assemblies. Politics and Ritual (1986) is the earlier collection identified independently by KCL. This records her explicit methodological account, not membership in a single school; neither the collection nor her cited historiographical chapter was read in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her funeral address quoted in David d’Avray and John Hudson’s memoir of Susan Reynolds (2022), Janet Nelson credits discussions with Reynolds with helping her refine and develop historical ideas.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: British Academy memoir (2022), p. 164, quotes Nelson’s funeral address and explicitly identifies their repeated historical discussions. This is a stated intellectual debt, with Reynolds as source and Nelson as recipient; no particular Nelson book is identified. The KCL profile additionally confirms their coediting of Gender and Historiography (2012), retained as supplementary bibliographic evidence.
proposed_edges.map_label: Nelson credits Reynolds with developing ideas

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Dispute Settlement in Carolingian West Francia” (1986), Nelson challenged accounts of Carolingian government centred on top-down control by showing the importance of local power, custom and participation in judicial decisions, as Wendy Davies explains in her 2025 retrospective.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Davies’s complete section in the journal’s open HTML. It identifies the 1986 essay and explains its challenge to state-centred justice. This is a political-history contribution, independently of the existing cultural-history pair; the underlying essay was not read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Writing Early Medieval Biography” (2000), Nelson argued that an early medieval life could be written when varied evidence illuminates the subject’s life stages and inner life and connects the individual to historical context, using Charlemagne as her case.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete publisher abstract and publication details, not the paywalled article. The abstract specifies varied genres, first-hand material, different life phases, inner life and contextual links, and states that Charlemagne meets these conditions. The claim is limited to this stated methodological argument.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Nelson’s King and Emperor: A New Life of Charlemagne (2019), Patrick J. Geary praised its involvement of readers in the historical investigation, comparing the resulting suspense to detective work, in the passage quoted by his institution.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete notice on Geary’s institutional site and the accessible opening three paragraphs of the linked newspaper review. The notice quotes his appraisal of the book’s method and identifies the review. The review’s remaining text was unavailable; this comparison records only that quoted appraisal and does not infer influence or the absence of criticism elsewhere.
